examples.text: Être en émoi, mettre en émoi.

glosses: Émotion plus ou moins troublante.

examples.text: Cette nuit, nous aperçûmes un voilier; cette rencontre était si extraordinaire dans ces parages infréquentés, qu'elle causa à bord un grand émoi ; toutes les lunettes étaient braquées sur le mystérieux navire.
On tourna le dos à l'Hôtel des monnaies, la vainqueresse musardait, feignant de rien deviner de mes émois ni de la captivité dans laquelle, d'un inimitable balancement fessier, elle m'avait jeté.
Entre les mains de Chantal, la pomme de la douche s’animait, devenait complice de tendres émois.

glosses: Any sound or information intended to give notice of approaching danger; a warning sound to arouse attention; a warning of danger.

examples.text: Sound an alarm in my holy mountain.
She went about the house in a state of real terror, and yet lied monstrously and wilfully, and invented many of the alarms she spread, and made many of the sounds we heard.

glosses: A device intended to warn or give notice of approaching danger.

examples.text: The fire alarm is located high on the wall to prevent tampering.

glosses: A sudden attack; a disturbance.

examples.text:
Lord Marshal, command our officers-at-arms
Be ready to direct these home alarms.

Is it then true, as distant rumours run,
that crowds of rivals for thy mother's charms
thy Palace fill with insults and alarms?

glosses: Sudden surprise with fear or terror excited by apprehension of danger; in the military use, commonly, sudden apprehension of being attacked by surprise.

examples.text: Alarm and resentment spread through the camp.

glosses: A mechanical device for awaking people, or rousing their attention.

examples.text: The clock radio is a friendlier version of the cold alarm by the bedside.

glosses: An instance of an alarm ringing, beeping or clanging, to give a noise signal at a certain time.

examples.text: You should set the alarm on your watch to go off at seven o'clock.

glosses: To call to arms for defense.
To give (someone) notice of approaching danger or necessary action; to rouse to vigilance; to put on the alert.

examples.text: The sudden drop in temperature should alarm you into taking precautions.
Her illness started to alarm the doctors, who ordered more tests.

When the carriage drew up in the grass-grown court yard before the hall-door, two lazy-looking men, whose appearance well accorded with that of the place which they tenanted, alarmed by the obstreperous barking of a great chained dog, ran out from some half-ruinous out-houses, and took charge of the horses; […]

glosses: To produce a warning of approaching danger or necessary action; to emit a signal intended to rouse a recipient to vigilance or put them on the alert.

examples.text: The tower cab supervisor and various pilots stated that the LLWAS system frequently alarms because of the thunderstorm activity present, and that airspeed losses are common as a result of convective wind shear.

glosses: To surprise with apprehension of danger; to fill with anxiety in regard to threatening evil; to excite with sudden fear.

examples.text: The loud bang in the hallway seemed to alarm everyone in the building.

glosses: To keep in excitement; to disturb.
A state of great disorder or uncertainty.

examples.text: Oleg Blokhin's side lost the talismanic Andriy Shevchenko to the substitutes' bench because of a knee injury but still showed enough to put England through real turmoil in spells.

glosses: Harassing labor; trouble; disturbance.

examples.text: And there I'll rest, as after much turmoil, / A blessed soul doth in Elysium.

The turmoil went on—no rest, no peace. […] It was nearly eleven o'clock now, and he strolled out again. In the little fair created by the costers' barrows the evening only seemed beginning; and the naphtha flares made one's eyes ache, the men's voices grated harshly, and the girls' faces saddened one.

glosses: To be disquieted or confused; to be in commotion.

glosses: To harass with commotion; to disquiet; to worry.

examples.text: It is her fatal misfortune […] to be thus miserably tossed and turmoiled with these storms of affliction.
